summary:
Uruguay's trans-protection regime rests on the Comprehensive Law for Trans People (Law No. 19684), dated 26 October 2018 and promulgated by the Executive, which sets out state-guaranteed identity, health and anti-discrimination rights for trans persons. It provides legal gender recognition by administrative self-declaration, with no surgery or diagnosis required, alongside a reparation pension for trans victims of institutional violence and a state employment quota for trans people.

Same-sex relations are legal nationwide, and same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013. Uruguay was the first country in Latin America to recognise same-sex civil unions, in legislation signed by President Tabaré Vázquez in December 2007 that gave couples cohabiting five years or more rights equivalent to marriage.

Non-discrimination protection, a ban on conversion therapy, an equal age of consent and hate-crime rules covering sexual orientation and gender identity are all in force. The status grid compiled for Montevideo reflects national law rather than any municipal rule, so the same baseline applies elsewhere in the country.

Detention is governed by an explicit placement right: the National Rehabilitation Institute states that a trans person entering the prison system may decide whether to be held in a men's or a women's prison, and trans women are currently placed in women's prisons. A new prison under construction in Montevideo will include a dedicated sector for trans inmates, and the new women's prison at Punta de Rieles will for the first time account for the trans population. The Parliamentary Commissioner for the Prison System recorded 28 trans women and nine trans men among 14,965 people deprived of liberty.

Lethal violence against trans people continues despite that framework. Joana, a 29-year-old trans woman, was shot dead in her home in Montevideo on 28 July 2025; a suspect was subsequently sentenced to seven years for the murder, giving the case judicial follow-through.

Discrimination complaints in public services are being litigated. In May 2024 the trans health-service user Andreina Stuart denounced mistreatment and discrimination at the hospital in San Carlos, Maldonado; a criminal complaint is pending, the hospital director pledged an administrative investigation once the judicial stage concludes, and local officials pressed for updates to the health system. Beccah Rivas, a trans woman, has sued the state bank BROU over discriminatory handling by a Prosegur guard and alleges the bank withheld the key camera footage; prosecutor Tania Vidal compelled the bank to produce material, and Rivas says she was dismissed after publicising the case.

Outright's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, records same-sex relations legal, legal gender recognition available and LGBTI organisations registrable as the civil-rights baseline a visitor enters, while flagging intersex bodily-autonomy protections as incomplete.
tangentialFactors:
Freedom House rated Uruguay Free in its 2024 Freedom in the World report at 96/100, with political rights at 40/40 and civil liberties at 56/60, a general rights climate that sits behind the trans-specific statutes rather than replacing them.

The gap between statute and practice is acknowledged by the authorities themselves. National Rehabilitation Institute Director Luis Mendoza told a parliamentary hearing that the laws are very advanced in Uruguay but that mentality and infrastructure are not in line, noting that housing trans women in female prisons entails a whole process of adaptation. Parliamentary Commissioner Juan Miguel Petit called the planned trans sector good news for a very vulnerable population and estimated it would be ready in under two years.

Intersex bodily-autonomy protections remain incomplete even where LGB and trans provisions are in place, so the umbrella term LGBTI covers uneven ground in this jurisdiction.

Enforcement outcomes vary across the documented cases: a murder produced a seven-year sentence, a hospital complaint sits at the criminal-complaint stage with an administrative investigation deferred behind it, and a discrimination suit against a state bank has turned on disclosure of evidence.
localsOnly:
Law No. 19684 operates as resident-facing statute as well as visitor protection: it guarantees identity, health and anti-discrimination rights, and it carries a state employment quota for trans people plus a reparation pension for trans victims of institutional violence.

Legal gender recognition is administrative and based on self-declaration, so residents can change their registered gender without surgical or psychiatric prerequisites.

LGBTI organisations can be registered, which underpins the domestic advocacy and service infrastructure available to residents.

Prison placement is a right exercisable by residents: the National Rehabilitation Institute holds that a trans person entering the system may choose between a men's and a women's prison, and the new women's prison at Punta de Rieles is designed to account for the trans population for the first time. Official counts list 28 trans women and nine trans men among 14,965 people deprived of liberty.

Residents pursuing complaints through the courts face open proceedings: Andreina Stuart's criminal complaint against the San Carlos hospital is pending, and Beccah Rivas's suit against BROU is contested over the production of camera footage, with a prosecutor having compelled disclosure.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Equaldex status grid for Montevideo is an undated compiled page; the underlying dates of the non-discrimination, conversion-therapy and hate-crime provisions are not sourced here and remain unresolved.

Whether the dedicated trans sector in the new Montevideo prison has been completed is unresolved: the July 2023 report gives an official estimate of under two years, and no later confirmation appears in the inventory.

The outcome of Andreina Stuart's criminal complaint and of the hospital's promised administrative investigation is not sourced beyond the pending stage reported in May 2024.

The disposition of Beccah Rivas's discrimination suit against BROU, and the veracity of her allegation that footage was withheld, are unresolved; only the prosecutor's compulsion of material and her dismissal claim are documented.

The motive in the killing of Joana, and whether the homicide was prosecuted or treated as a hate crime, are not sourced; only the seven-year sentence is recorded.

The scope of the incomplete intersex bodily-autonomy protections flagged by Outright is not specified in the inventory.
